text: Every other pattern in this chapter answers "how do we handle a change?" SCD Type 0 answers a different question: what happens when an attribute must never change, no matter what the source system says.

Picture a customer's very first purchase date. The source system's other data changes constantly, but that one value shouldn't move — it's a fixed historical fact the moment it's recorded. That's Type 0: the ETL process loads it once, at insert, and then deliberately never writes an update against that column again, ever, regardless of what the source says later.

The risk is that Type 0 looks identical to simply forgetting to write an update statement — which means a future "refresh everything" ETL change can silently overwrite a value that was supposed to be permanent, with no error and no one noticing. The fix is to make the rule explicit in code: this column is excluded from every load's SET list, on every run, forever — not just the one you happen to be writing today.
Type 0 and Type 1, coming up next, can look identical in the table — one row, no history — but they differ completely in intent. Type 1 next.
